    Instructor Notes

    Overview

    This module (Training Material 6: Statistical programming for bibliographic data science) uses the Fennica national bibliography (1809–1917) as a single running example. It covers preprocessing, harmonisation, validation and analysis. Learners are expected to know basic R (running scripts, loading packages, importing data, simple data-frame operations); no prior experience with bibliographic data is required. Episodes 2–4 (Meet the Fennica Data, harmonisation and validation) form Part 1 of the course: from raw records to analysis-ready, validated data. The analysis episodes are being redesigned to lead from descriptive statistics to statistical models and probabilistic analysis.

    Before the workshop

    • Ask learners to complete the Setup in advance. Installing arrow can take a while on some systems.
    • Have the data file available on a USB stick or shared drive in case of slow internet.
    • Test that arrow::read_ipc_file() works on the workshop machines.

    Episode notes

    Introduction to the Course

    • Introduce the running question and the course stages (table in the episode). Many learners know library catalogues but not MARC 21: walk through the example record field by field.
    • Challenge 1 (reading a real record) prepares the harmonisation episode: the place is in field 264, not 260, and field 008 hides the year.
    • Challenge 2 is a discussion; it works well in pairs, especially with participants from other countries.
    • Demonstrate RStudio projects live: most later file path problems come from not working inside the project.

    Meet the Fennica Data

    • Challenge 2 (swapped columns) is a good moment for discussion: how would you notice this in your own data? The validation episode returns to it.

    The running question

    Episodes 4 onwards follow one question: how did the shift from Swedish to Finnish in publishing happen, and how certain can we be about it? Return to it at the start and end of every episode. The harmonisation and validation episodes build the variables (language, place, publisher, author) and show that the answer depends on data decisions; later parts of the course quantify that uncertainty.

    Preprocessing and Harmonisation (about 80 minutes)

    • Uses the raw records priority_fields19.feather (all 72,626 records; the id matches the harmonised data exactly). Columns are named, but the episode maps each to its MARC field.
    • Rhythm for every field: profile, find a pattern, clean with a function, count again. Each field ends as a function; the episode ends with harmonise_records(), which is also in files/harmonise_fennica.R.
    • Key teaching moments:
      • Two sources for the same information: 041 vs 008 for language, 260 vs 264 for place. Combine them with coalesce().
      • Mikkeli (Challenge 2): field 264 of about 8,650 digitised copies gives the National Library’s digitisation centre in Mikkeli as the place. Let learners discover this themselves; it is the central “a clean value can measure the wrong thing” example.
      • Synonym table: entries are partly ASCII-folded (abo, borga), hence fold(). Unmatched values include Russian forms and Finnish emigrant presses in the USA.
      • Authority IDs: asteri_id separates the Runebergs and the two Alexandre Dumas. Among records with an ID there are more persons than name strings.
    • Regular expressions are new to many learners: build each pattern live on the small places vector first.
    • If time is short, skip the publisher section.

    Validation (about 70 minutes)

    • Three kinds of validation: rules, comparison with an independent harmonisation (the project’s file), and consequences for the research question.
    • Rule failures lead back to raw records: numbers as author names, dates in the name field (|), and S.l/S.a in the publisher field.
    • The comparison shows several problems in the project’s harmonised file:
      • its place and publisher columns are swapped;
      • it keeps language-specific place names (Helsingfors vs Helsinki);
      • Turku appears as a publisher for “… i Finland” societies;
      • polish_author() reverses patronymics (Ragvaldinpoika, Thomas).
    • Missingness: Swedish records lack a publisher (52%) and a place (21%) more often than Finnish ones (30% and 16%). The sensitivity plot shows the Finnish share by decade for four subsets. Restricting to records with a known publisher moves the 50% crossing from the 1870s to the 1850s.
    • Challenge 3 (Helsinki vs Helsingfors: 95% vs 4% Finnish) prepares the later modelling episodes: a raw place name is partly the outcome itself.
    • The 1810s value is inflated by questionable dates; this is left for the publication-time episode.
    • The lookup tables in episodes/data/ are from inst/extdata of the fennica package (BSD-2 licence).

    From the harmonised data to fennica_clean

    • The analysis episodes use fennica_clean, created from the project’s harmonised file by files/clean_fennica.R (swap fixed, places merged, English genre labels).
    • Further findings from running the real polish_*() functions: polish_author_years() turns syntynyt 1875 (“born 1875”) into birth = death = 1875 (the “age zero” authors in the visualisation episode), and the harmonised title column is the uniform title (field 240).

    Summarising Data

    • Stress the difference between counts and proportions; the language shift from Swedish to Finnish is the key historical story.

    Visualising Data with ggplot2

    • Build plots incrementally, adding one layer at a time.
    • The faceting example with scales = "free_y" is a good prompt to discuss how plot choices can mislead.

    Basic Statistical Analysis

    • Learners may have no statistics background. Focus on interpretation rather than formulas.
    • The key messages are: medians for skewed data, correlation is not causation, and with large data effect sizes matter more than p-values.

    Known data issues

    • publisher and publication_place are swapped in the source data; this is discovered in the validation episode.
    • title2 contains a "Na " prefix when title is missing.
    • genre_008 contains character-set values (e.g. “Laajennettu latinalainen”).
    • The page count and physical dimension columns are mostly empty or unreliable and are not used in the lesson.
    • Decade 1800 contains only records from 1809, and the 1910s end in 1917.
